rationale: Ectodermal manifestations—most notably thin or sparse hair (reported in 26/28 individuals, ~92.9%) along with dental anomalies—are prominent hallmark features of GTPBP2-related Jaberi-Elahi syndrome that provide powerful discriminating value against pure neurodegenerative phenocopies like PLA2G6-associated infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy (PLAN). However, designating ectodermal features as 'mandatory' criteria is refuted by the clinical natural history: 2 of 28 individuals in published cohorts lacked sparse hair, Carter et al. established that ectodermal findings are age-dependent and evolve over time (becoming most prominent in older individuals), and recent infant case reports (e.g., a 4-month-old infant with confirmed biallelic GTPBP2 loss-of-function) presented with no overt ectodermal abnormalities.

evidence.text: In a comprehensive review of 28 patients with Jaberi-Elahi syndrome, sparse hair was documented in 26 of 28 patients (92.9%), alongside motor development delay (26/28), speech disorder (24/28), intellectual disability (23/28), and hypotonia (23/28).

source.title: Jaberi-Elahi syndrome: Exploring a novel GTPBP2 mutation and a literature review
source.quote: A large numbers of patients manifest motor development delay (26/28), sparse hair (26/28), and speech disorder (24/28). Moreover, a significant fraction of patients suffer from intellectual disability (23/28), hypotonia (23/28), skeletal problems (23/28), and visual impairment (18/28).

evidence.text: Phenotypic delineation indicates that ectodermal dysplasia and brain iron accumulation are key features, but ectodermal findings and peripheral neuropathy are age-related and most prominent in older individuals, indicating they may not be detectable in early infancy.

source.title: Clinical delineation of GTPBP2‐associated neuro‐ectodermal syndrome: Report of two new families and review of the literature
source.quote: Our findings suggest that some aspects of the clinical presentation appear to be age-related; brain iron accumulation may appear only after childhood, and the ectodermal findings and peripheral neuropathy are most prominent in older individuals.

evidence.text: A 4-month-old female infant with confirmed homozygous pathogenic GTPBP2 frameshift mutation presented with severe microcephaly, developmental delay, hypotonia, and white matter abnormalities, but no overt ectodermal abnormalities were observed.

source.title: Jaberi-Elahi syndrome - NIH Genetic Testing Registry (GTR)
source.quote: We report a 4-month-old female infant born to consanguineous parents, presenting with severe microcephaly, developmental delay, hypotonia, and craniofacial features... No overt ectodermal abnormalities were observed.

evidence.text: GTPBP2 is classified as a causative etiology of neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation (NBIA), a category shared with PLA2G6 (associated with PLAN), highlighting marked clinical overlap in tone abnormalities, pyramidal signs, and movement disorders.

source.title: Neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation
source.quote: GTPBP2 mutations are another rare cause of NBIA, sometimes referred to as Jaberi–Elahi syndrome... Numerous different mutations in the PLA2G6 gene (associated with PLAN)

conflicts: The hypothesis asserts that ectodermal findings are 'mandatory' criteria to discriminate Jaberi-Elahi syndrome from phenocopies; however, ectodermal findings are absent in at least 7.1% (2/28) of reported literature cohort patients and were explicitly absent on exam in a confirmed 4-month-old infant carrying a homozygous frameshift variant.

Carter et al. demonstrated that ectodermal features are progressive and age-dependent, meaning younger infants cannot be distinguished from INAD/PLAN or pontocerebellar hypoplasias relying strictly on mandatory ectodermal manifestations.

new_directions.question_text: What is the earliest postnatal age at which ectodermal findings (hypotrichosis, sparse eyebrows, abnormal dentition) manifest in GTPBP2 patients?
new_directions.rationale: Clarifying the temporal onset of ectodermal features across longitudinal cohorts will determine age-stratified sensitivity of ectodermal criteria in distinguishing Jaberi-Elahi syndrome from infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy.

new_directions.question_text: Does electroretinography (ERG) or early funduscopy provide higher discriminative diagnostic yield than ectodermal examination during the first year of life?
new_directions.rationale: Retinal dystrophy is another core distinguishing feature of GTPBP2 deficiency that may precede overt ectodermal manifestations and assist in early clinical distinction from PLA2G6.
